title: Burst Balloons
statement: You get a row of balloons, each with a number. Bursting a balloon scores its number times the numbers of its two current neighbours. A missing neighbour counts as 1. Burst all balloons in the best order and return the largest total score.

example.caption: For 3, 1, 5 the best plan is to burst the 1 first, then the 3, then the 5. Each score is a product of the balloon and its neighbours at that moment.

idea.sentence: Instead of asking which balloon to burst first, ask which one is burst last in a range: then its two sides are independent, and dp[l][r] = best of dp[l][k] + a[l]*a[k]*a[r] + dp[k][r].

jargon.plain: A table over ranges of the input. A long range is solved from the shorter ranges inside it, so we fill short ranges first.
If k is burst last in a range, its neighbours at that moment are the fixed edges l and r, because everything between has already gone.

watch.inputHint: One argument: a list of balloon numbers. Keep it to 3 or 4 balloons, because every choice of last balloon is a step.

compare.unit: steps (brute force really grows as n factorial, drawn as the closest shape)

rows.name: Try every burst order
rows.note: Every order of the n balloons is a different plan. The neighbours change as balloons vanish, so plans cannot be combined.

rows.name: Interval DP, last balloon
rows.note: About n^2/2 ranges, and each tries up to n choices of last balloon.

fast.takeaway: Choosing the last balloon makes the two sides independent. That turns a tangle of orders into n squared ranges with n choices each.

stages.title: Pad with ones
stages.note: Add a 1 at each end so the first and last balloon have neighbours. The table is n by n over the padded row.

stages.title: Short ranges first
stages.note: Loop over the gap r - l from 2 upward, so every smaller range inside is already filled.

stages.title: Try each last balloon
stages.note: For every k between l and r, k is burst last: its score is a[l]*a[k]*a[r] plus the two sides dp[l][k] and dp[k][r].

stages.title: Keep the best
stages.note: dp[l][r] is the largest total over all choices of k.

stages.title: Read the corner
stages.note: Range (0, n-1) holds every real balloon. dp[0][n-1] is the answer.

edges.title: No balloons
edges.why: The padded row is [1, 1] and no range has anything inside. The loops never run and dp[0][1] is 0.

edges.title: One balloon
edges.why: Its neighbours are the two padded ones, so the score is 1 * 5 * 1.

edges.title: A zero balloon
edges.why: Burst the 0 first: it scores 0 and leaves 3 and 5 side by side. Then 3 scores 1*3*5 = 15 and 5 scores 5. A 0 is a free way to join its neighbours.

edges.title: All zeros
edges.why: Every product has a zero in it. All table cells stay 0, so a max starting from 0 is fine.

gotchas.text: Do not model it as the first balloon to burst. Then the neighbours of the two sides depend on each other and the ranges are not independent. The last-burst view keeps the edges l and r fixed.
The range (l, r) is open: l and r themselves are not burst. The loop for k runs from l+1 to r-1 and the answer is dp[0][n-1] on the padded row.
Array.from({ length: n }, () => new Array(n).fill(0)) gives each row its own array. new Array(n).fill(new Array(n).fill(0)) would make every row the same array.
make([][]int, n) has nil rows. Allocate each row. Build the padded slice with a fresh make and append, so you never write into the caller's nums by accident.

Each burst scores a product of three numbers, so totals grow fast. With values up to 100 and a few hundred balloons the sum is in the hundreds of millions. Go int and JavaScript numbers hold it, a narrower integer type may not.

recap.pattern: Interval DP, pick the last element
recap.key: dp[l][r] is the max over k in (l, r) of dp[l][k] + a[l]*a[k]*a[r] + dp[k][r], with k burst last.
moves: Pad the array with 1 on both ends
Loop gap from 2 up so short ranges come first
For each k try k as the last balloon burst
Keep the max in dp[l][r], answer dp[0][n-1]
